aurelia_gold.name: Gold Allocation
aurelia_gold.summary: Adjusts how much is held in a gold fund, following the same signal system as the Nasdaq allocation.
aurelia_gold.explainer: This strategy watches a single gold signal supplied to the desk, which says how much exposure to gold is wanted, alongside a separate Nasdaq signal that shares the same overall pot of money. It buys shares in a fund that holds physical gold when the gold signal has moved at least 0.20 away from what is currently held. Gold is held one-for-one, with no borrowed or multiplied exposure, and the combined Nasdaq and gold holdings are kept within a shared limit. It sells gold fund shares when the signal falls, and it sells all of them when the gold signal reaches zero.

aurelia_ndx.name: Nasdaq Allocation
aurelia_ndx.summary: Adjusts how much is held in Nasdaq funds, using a triple-strength fund for exposure above 100%.
aurelia_ndx.explainer: This strategy watches a single Nasdaq strength signal supplied to the desk, which says how much exposure to large US technology-heavy stocks is wanted, from none upward. It buys when that signal has moved at least 0.20 away from what is currently held, or buys a new holding whenever its target changes. Exposure up to 100% is held in a Nasdaq fund; above that, part moves into a fund that moves three times as much. At least 2% sits in a short-term Treasury fund when money is left over. It sells when the signal falls, and it sells everything in this part when the signal reaches zero.

beatendown.name: Beaten-Down Winners
beatendown.summary: Buys screened past winners that have fallen at least 20% from their 52-week high, then holds for 13 weeks.
beatendown.explainer: It watches a weekly screen of stocks that have already passed the desk's quality and strength checks, looking for ones whose price has been beaten down to 80% or less of their highest weekly close of the past 52 weeks — at least 20% below the high. Among those, it ranks candidates by how many of nine frozen winner patterns are present at once, combining things like big weekly moves, leadership within their industry group, and strong momentum readings; there is no minimum count, the count only sets the order. It holds at most ten positions, pauses new buys around Federal Reserve meetings and at year-end, and sells each holding after 91 days, about 13 weeks. It trades US stocks.

bilbo_options.name: Compression Breakout Calls
bilbo_options.summary: Buys a call option when a large, well-known stock breaks upward out of a tight hourly price range.
bilbo_options.explainer: This strategy watches 20 U.S. stocks on hourly charts for periods when price squeezes into a tight, compressed range. The first five compressed hours form a range, watched for up to ten days. It buys one call option — a contract giving the right to buy the stock at an agreed price by an agreed date; it gains when the price rises — when the first hour out of the squeeze closes above that range's high, between 10 a.m. and 3 p.m. on a weekday, with the stock above its 21-day average. The call expires in 21 to 37 days, aimed above the current price. It sells if price closes below the range's low, gives back most of a large gain, after ten trading days, or near expiry (the date the option runs out). It trades stock options.

capitulation.name: Capitulation Reversal
capitulation.summary: Buys the first sign of a turnaround after a panic sell-off climax, in halves, and exits fast.
capitulation.explainer: It watches hourly price bars, hunting for a panic climax: an hourly momentum gauge below 20, trading volume on the climax bar more than double the previous 20 bars, a low within 2% of the stock's 200-day average price, and big daily swings — average daily movement above 5%. It buys at the close of the first rising bar after the climax, once momentum turns up, taking half the position first and adding the rest when the 5-day average turns up through the 20-day average within five sessions. It sells at the first of: price up to the day's average traded price, a 5% gain, an 8% loss, or three trading days, and a safety stop closes the trade if the price falls 25% from entry. It trades US stocks.

capitulation_options.name: Capitulation Reversal Calls
capitulation_options.summary: Buys a short-dated call option when a stock shows signs of a panic sell-off ending and starting to recover.
capitulation_options.explainer: This strategy watches U.S. stocks for a five-part sign that a panic sell-off is ending: hourly momentum fell below 20, an extreme reading; selling volume was more than twice the previous 20 hours; the low landed within 2% of the stock's 200-day average; the next hourly bar turned green with momentum rising; and the stock's daily price swings exceed 5% of its price. When all five align, it buys one call option — a call gains in value when the price rises — expiring within seven days, priced about 2% above the current stock price. It sells when the option gains 75%, when one day remains before expiry (the date the option runs out), or if the stock falls 3% from entry. It trades stock options.

confluence.name: Winner Confluence
confluence.summary: Buys screened stocks where at least two of nine winner patterns line up at once, then holds for 13 weeks.
confluence.explainer: It watches a weekly screen of stocks that have passed the desk's quality and strength checks, and scores each one against nine frozen winner patterns. Each pattern combines three ingredients — things like a big weekly price move, leadership within its industry group, a weak dollar backdrop, and strong momentum readings. It buys only when at least two of the nine patterns are firing on the same stock, and it ranks candidates by how many are firing, most first. It holds at most ten positions and pauses new buys around Federal Reserve meetings and in the last sessions of the year. It sells each holding after 91 days, about 13 weeks. It trades US stocks.

daily_cyan_gbm.name: Daily Model Score
daily_cyan_gbm.summary: Buys the stocks a machine-learning model scores highest each day, and holds each one for 21 trading sessions.
daily_cyan_gbm.explainer: It watches daily market data across a broad stock universe and feeds those features into a machine-learning model that gives every stock a score each day, grading how attractive its recent pattern looks compared with everything the model has learned. It buys when a stock's score clears a high bar — roughly the top tenth of all scores — and the stock trades at 5 dollars or more, taking the highest scores first. There is no signal from a single chart pattern here; the model's ranking is the signal. It sells each holding at the close of the 21st trading session after purchase, whatever the price has done in between. It trades US stocks.

donchian.name: Donchian Breakout
donchian.summary: A classic trend-following breakout strategy: buy a close above the 20-day high, ride it, exit below the 10-day low.
donchian.explainer: Named for Richard Donchian, this approach simply watches the highest and lowest prices over a set period: it tracks daily high, low and closing prices across the desk's stock basket, tracking each stock's highest high of the last 20 days and lowest low of the last 10 days. It buys when a stock closes above that 20-day high — a genuine breakout to new ground. Once in, it follows the trend with a trailing stop set at twice the stock's typical daily price movement below the price. It sells when the stock closes below its 10-day low, when that trailing stop is reached, or after 20 trading days, and a safety stop also sells any holding that falls 25% from its purchase price. It holds at most eight positions at a time. It trades US stocks.

donchian_crypto.name: Solana Donchian Breakout
donchian_crypto.summary: The same classic breakout rules, run on Solana in 15-minute bars, one position at a time.
donchian_crypto.explainer: Named for Richard Donchian, this approach watches Solana's price in 15-minute bars around the clock (a bar is one period's price summary — where it opened, its high, its low, and where it closed), tracking the highest high of the last 20 bars and the lowest low of the last 10 bars once at least 40 bars are available. It buys when Solana closes above that 20-bar high, a breakout — an equal high does not count — and only when the breakout bar traded volume. It holds a single position at a time and there is no time limit on a trade. It sells when the price closes below the 10-bar low, or when the low of a bar touches a trailing stop set at twice Solana's typical price movement, whichever happens first. It trades crypto on paper only.

earnings_buyback.name: Buyback Before Earnings
earnings_buyback.summary: Buys options on a company that recently announced a large share buyback, shortly before its earnings report.
earnings_buyback.explainer: This strategy watches company announcements for a share buyback of at least 5% of the company, filed 15 to 30 days before a scheduled earnings report, in stocks priced at $10 or more. It buys eight to fifteen days before earnings, using options that expire 30 to 45 days out and always after the report, so the position is held through earnings. It prefers a two-part call spread about 10% wide (a call gains in value when the price rises; a spread pairs a bought option with a sold one, capping the most that can be made or lost), and otherwise buys a single call about 2% above the current price. It sells 15 trading days after earnings, when the trade gains 50%, if it loses 50%, or with five days left before expiry. It trades stock options.

ema_vwap.name: VWAP Pullback
ema_vwap.summary: Buys stocks trading at least 2% below their 20-day average traded price (VWAP — the day's average traded price, weighted by how much traded at each price), expecting a snap back to that average.
ema_vwap.explainer: It watches daily prices across the desk's stock basket and keeps a running 20-day average of each stock's traded price, weighted by volume — that average is the VWAP in the strategy's name, the price level where most recent trading actually happened. It buys when a stock's latest close sits at least 2% below that average, treating the gap as a short-term overreaction. It sells as soon as the price climbs back to or above that average price, its main exit. It also sells at a 5% gain, an 8% loss, or after five trading days, and a safety stop sells any holding down 25% from its purchase price. It holds at most eight positions at a time. It trades US stocks.

ema_vwap_options.name: Below-Average-Price Call Spreads
ema_vwap_options.summary: Buys a two-part call spread when a stock has fallen at least 2% below its recent average traded price.
ema_vwap_options.explainer: This strategy watches U.S. stocks day by day, comparing each stock's closing price with its average traded price over the past 20 days, weighted by how much stock changed hands. It buys a call spread — a call gains in value when the price rises, and a spread pairs a bought option with a sold one, with limited cost and limited profit — when the close sits at least 2% below that average, betting on a bounce back. The spread uses options expiring in 14 to 30 days, bought about 2% above the current price and sold about 6% higher. It sells when the spread reaches half its maximum profit, when price climbs back to that average, after 21 days, or with seven days left before expiry (the date the option runs out). It trades stock options.

fear_premium.name: Fear Premium Put Spreads
fear_premium.summary: Sells a two-part put spread after a sharp one-day drop in a fast-moving stock, collecting the premium — the payment received for selling an option — for the fear.
fear_premium.explainer: This strategy watches the ten stocks that move the most compared with the Nasdaq-100 fund over the past 60 days, plus two aggressive leveraged funds that are always included. After a stock falls at least 5% in a single day and its 14-day momentum reading is below 50, it sells a put spread — a put gains in value when the price falls, and a spread is a paired option trade that collects payment upfront with limited risk — using options expiring in 25 to 35 days. The sold put sits about 7% below the closing price, with a protective bought put about 10% lower. It closes the trade at half its maximum profit, after eight days, or with 21 days left before expiry (the date the option runs out). It trades stock options.

free_etf.name: Scheduled ETF Baskets
free_etf.summary: Buys set baskets of exchange-traded funds in fixed proportions, on a set schedule near the market open.
free_etf.explainer: This strategy watches set baskets of exchange-traded funds, each with fixed proportions for its holdings, and checks that a full year, 252 trading days, of daily price history is available for every fund in a basket. It buys only between 9:35 and 9:40 a.m. Eastern, on scheduled days at the start of a basket and in the first five trading days of a month, and only when the gap between buying and selling prices is small. Spending is capped at $25,000 in a day. It sells when a holding is above its target proportion, and those sales can happen outside the morning buying window.

free_kraken_ada_basis.name: Cardano Price Alignment Monitor
free_kraken_ada_basis.summary: Watches whether Cardano's futures-style and cash prices on Kraken line up, and records the result — it never places a trade.
free_kraken_ada_basis.explainer: This strategy watches Cardano, known as ADA, on the Kraken exchange, comparing its futures-style contract price with its cash market price to check that the two line up. The long price history it would need for that check is not currently collected, so today it cannot complete the comparison. It never buys and never sells: there is no buy trigger and no exit rule, because placing trades was never part of its job. Instead, each hour it records a status saying the history it needs is not available yet, so the gap is visible rather than hidden. It tracks crypto on paper.

free_kraken_ada_breakdown.name: Cardano Breakdown Short
free_kraken_ada_breakdown.summary: Sells Cardano short on paper when its price breaks below its lowest level of the past 20 four-hour periods.
free_kraken_ada_breakdown.explainer: This strategy watches Cardano, a cryptocurrency, in four-hour price periods on the Kraken exchange, using its dollar perpetual contract, which tracks the price without an expiry date. It sells short, meaning it bets on a fall, when a four-hour period closes below the lowest low of the previous 20 periods, about three and a third days. The sale happens eight hours after that period opened, at a live quoted price, and is for one contract on paper only. It buys back to close the position 16 hours after the entry was due, whatever the price has done by then.

free_kraken_ada_crowded.name: Cardano Crowded Breakdown Short
free_kraken_ada_crowded.summary: Sells Cardano short on Kraken only when its price breaks down and buyers look crowded, then covers 16 hours later.
free_kraken_ada_crowded.explainer: This strategy watches Cardano, known as ADA, through a futures-style contract on the Kraken exchange, using four-hour price bars plus an hourly cost that traders pay to hold long positions (long means owned — a position that gains when the price rises). It sells short, a bet that the price will fall, only when two things line up: a bar closes below the lowest low of the previous 20 bars, and buyers look crowded — the latest hourly funding cost is above zero and higher than three quarters of the past 90 days of readings, with at least 30 readings on record. The trade is one contract, and it buys back to close 16 hours after entry. It trades crypto on paper.

free_kraken_enj_spot.name: Enjin Spot Watch on Kraken
free_kraken_enj_spot.summary: Watches Enjin Coin's live cash market on Kraken and records its best prices, but never places a trade.
free_kraken_enj_spot.explainer: This strategy watches Enjin Coin, known as ENJ, on the Kraken exchange, checking the live list of buy and sell offers for the coin priced in US dollars. It is a watch-only strategy, because ENJ has no futures-style contract on Kraken, only a cash market. So it never opens a buy or a short trade, and there is no sell or exit rule to run. Instead, it records the best buy and sell prices when the order list is live and healthy. If that list is empty, or the best buy price sits above the best sell price, it records that the feed is not usable and takes no action. It tracks crypto on paper.

free_kraken_link_basis.name: Chainlink Price Alignment Monitor
free_kraken_link_basis.summary: Watches whether Chainlink's futures-style and cash prices on Kraken line up, and records the result — it never places a trade.
free_kraken_link_basis.explainer: This strategy watches Chainlink, known as LINK, on the Kraken exchange, comparing its futures-style contract price with its cash market price to check that the two line up. The long price history it would need for that check is not currently collected, so today it cannot complete the comparison. It never buys and never sells: there is no buy trigger and no exit rule, because placing trades was never part of its job. Instead, each hour it records a status saying the history it needs is not available yet, so the gap is visible rather than hidden. It tracks crypto on paper.

free_kraken_link_breakdown.name: Chainlink Breakdown Short on Kraken
free_kraken_link_breakdown.summary: Sells Chainlink short on Kraken after its price breaks below the lowest low of the past 20 four-hour bars, then covers 16 hours later.
free_kraken_link_breakdown.explainer: This strategy watches Chainlink, known as LINK, through a futures-style contract on the Kraken exchange, using four-hour price bars. It needs at least 22 completed bars before it acts. It opens a short trade, a bet that the price will fall, when a bar closes below the lowest low of the previous 20 bars. The trade starts eight hours after that signal bar opened, at a live quoted price, for one contract. It closes the short 16 hours after the entry time, whatever the price has done by then. It trades crypto on paper.

free_kraken_link_crowded.name: Chainlink Crowded Breakdown Short
free_kraken_link_crowded.summary: Sells Chainlink short on Kraken only when its price breaks down and buyers look crowded, then covers 16 hours later.
free_kraken_link_crowded.explainer: This strategy watches Chainlink, known as LINK, through a futures-style contract on the Kraken exchange, using four-hour price bars plus an hourly cost that traders pay to hold long positions (long means owned — a position that gains when the price rises). It sells short, a bet that the price will fall, only when two things line up: a bar closes below the lowest low of the previous 20 bars, and buyers look crowded — the latest hourly funding cost is above zero and higher than three quarters of the past 90 days of readings, with at least 30 readings on record. The trade is one contract, and it buys back to close 16 hours after entry. It trades crypto on paper.

free_opt_own_iv.name: Volatility Straddle
free_opt_own_iv.summary: Buys a call and a put together when expected price swings look larger than option prices suggest.
free_opt_own_iv.explainer: This strategy watches a forecast of how much a stock is likely to swing, compared with the swing level built into its option prices. It buys when that forecast is more than 2 points above the level in the option prices. It then buys both a call option, which gains if the stock rises, and a put option, which gains if it falls, at the same strike price — the agreed price at which the option lets you buy or sell — closest to the current stock price. Buying a call and a put together like this is called a straddle. The two are always bought together, never one alone. It sells both after ten trading sessions, or at expiry if that comes first.

free_opt_pair.name: Paired Options Trade
free_opt_pair.summary: Buys options on two different stocks together, sized using a ratio fixed in advance from past prices.
free_opt_pair.explainer: This strategy watches two different underlying stocks as a pair, and the balance between them, which is worked out in advance from their earlier closing prices and then frozen so it cannot shift mid-trade. It buys only when that balance has been frozen in advance and both sides of the pair are available together. It buys one option on each of the two stocks at the same time, so the trade is on the pair together rather than on either stock alone. If one side cannot be completed, the completed side is closed. It sells both sides after ten trading sessions.

free_opt_parity.name: Options Price Check
free_opt_parity.summary: Checks whether call and put prices line up fairly with each other, and never places a trade.
free_opt_parity.explainer: This strategy watches the prices of call and put options on the same stock, with the same strike price (the agreed price at which the option lets you buy or sell) and expiry date (the date the option runs out), and checks whether those prices line up with each other the way they normally should. A call gains when a stock rises and a put gains when it falls, so their prices are closely linked. It never triggers a buy: when it finds a gap between the two prices, it records what converting one position into the other would notionally cost, purely as a check. It never triggers a sell or exit either, because it holds no position. It trades no instruments.

free_opt_release.name: Verified Event Straddle
free_opt_release.summary: Buys a call and a put together only on a day with a verified public event for that stock.
free_opt_release.explainer: This strategy watches for a verified public event scheduled for today, such as a confirmed company announcement, using a checked event timestamp rather than a rumour or an unverified listing. It buys only when such a verified event is loaded for today's session. It then buys both a call option, which gains if the stock rises, and a put option, which gains if it falls, at the same strike price — the agreed price at which the option lets you buy or sell. Buying a call and a put together like this is called a straddle. The two are always bought together, never one alone. It sells both in the trading session after the event, or at expiry if that comes first.

free_opt_tail.name: Sharp Drop Put
free_opt_tail.summary: Buys one put option when a stock falls 3% or more in a single day.
free_opt_tail.explainer: This strategy watches how far a stock has fallen during the current trading day, looking for an unusually sharp drop rather than a slow drift lower. It buys when the stock is down 3% or more on the day and a fresh option price is available. It buys one put option, which gains in value if the stock keeps falling, so the position can help offset further losses. It sells the put after five trading sessions, if it has lost 50% of the premium paid for it (premium is simply the price paid for an option), or at expiry — the date the option runs out — if that comes first.

free_opt_wheel.name: Cash-Secured Put Wheel
free_opt_wheel.summary: Sells one put option only when enough cash is set aside to buy the shares if required.
free_opt_wheel.explainer: This strategy watches for put options it could sell while keeping enough cash aside to honour the sale in full. It sells one put option only when the cash set aside is at least the option's strike price (the agreed price at which the option lets you buy or sell) multiplied by 100, which is the full cost of buying 100 shares at that price. If the price falls and the shares are assigned — assigned means the seller must actually go through with buying the 100 shares at the strike price — the holder then owns those 100 shares. Later steps, including selling call options against shares owned this way, follow from that assignment rather than from this first sale. The 'wheel' is the repeating cycle of selling a put, possibly buying the shares, then selling calls against them.

fwd_alpaca_ada_rsi2.name: Cardano Oversold Bounce
fwd_alpaca_ada_rsi2.summary: Buys Cardano on hourly bars when a fast strength gauge drops below 10 while the price stays above its 200-bar average.
fwd_alpaca_ada_rsi2.explainer: This strategy watches Cardano, known as ADA, priced in US dollars, on one-hour price bars, and it needs 200 completed bars before it can act. It buys when a two-period strength gauge called RSI falls below 10, showing a sharp short-term drop, while the price still sits above its 200-bar average and below its 5-bar average, and the average of that gauge stays below 30. It acts only within five minutes of a bar closing, on a fresh quote. It sells when the price closes back above its 5-bar average. There is no emergency stop, and each trade uses up to 10% of the money set aside for it. It trades crypto on paper.

fwd_alpaca_enj_iu_body.name: Enjin Pair Watch
fwd_alpaca_enj_iu_body.summary: Set up for Enjin Coin priced in US dollars, but it places no trades because that pair is not listed on the exchange it checks.
fwd_alpaca_enj_iu_body.explainer: This strategy is set up to watch Enjin Coin, known as ENJ, priced in US dollars, but it currently places no trades at all. The pair it was built to trade is not listed on the exchange it checks, and no different coin is substituted in its place, so there is no buy trigger it can act on today. Because it never buys, it also has no sell or exit rule running. It simply stays blocked and reports why: the ENJ and US dollar pair cannot be found on that exchange. If the pair is ever listed, that would be a new decision, not an automatic start. It tracks crypto on paper.

fwd_alpaca_link_ai_volume.name: Chainlink Volume Surge
fwd_alpaca_link_ai_volume.summary: Buys Chainlink on four-hour bars when trading volume jumps above twice its average, then sells on the fifth bar.
fwd_alpaca_link_ai_volume.explainer: This strategy watches Chainlink, known as LINK, priced in US dollars, on four-hour price bars, and it needs 60 completed bars before it can act. It buys when trading volume rises above twice its smoothed average volume, while the price closes above its smoothed average price and above where that bar opened, a sign buyers stepped in with unusual force. It acts only within five minutes of a bar closing, and only on a fresh, orderly quote. It sells on the fifth completed bar of the trade, counting the bar it entered on, so each holding lasts about 20 hours. There is no emergency stop. It trades crypto on paper.

fwd_coinbase_sma200.name: Bitcoin Daily Buyer on Coinbase
fwd_coinbase_sma200.summary: Once a day, after checking 200 straight days of Bitcoin prices and a fresh quote, it buys a small fixed amount of Bitcoin.
fwd_coinbase_sma200.explainer: This strategy watches Bitcoin priced in US dollars on Coinbase, using daily price bars. Once a day, in the first five minutes after midnight UTC, it checks that it holds a full run of 200 completed daily bars in a row, with no missing days, and that it has a fresh price quote no more than 30 seconds old. When those checks pass, it buys a small fixed amount, 0.01 Bitcoin, once for that day, and the same day never triggers twice. It sets no profit target and has no built-in sell rule in its code, so holdings are closed only outside this strategy's own signals. It trades crypto on paper.

gate_1h.name: Daily Leader, Hourly Entry
gate_1h.summary: Takes the desk's strongest daily leadership signals and times the entry on hourly bars, holding for 20 hourly bars.
gate_1h.explainer: It watches daily prices for stocks with at least a year of trading history, looking for a leadership event: a day when a stock earns a high leadership score and passes the desk's daily strength test. When that event fires, it switches to hourly bars from regular market hours and buys on the first hourly bar after the event day, using the finer timeframe purely to time the entry. New entries in the same stock are spaced at least 20 hourly bars apart so one event cannot trigger repeated buys. It sells after 20 hourly bars in the trade, and a safety stop sells any holding that falls 25% below its purchase price. It holds at most ten positions. It trades US stocks.

iron_condor.name: Range-Bound Option Income
iron_condor.summary: Sells options on both sides of a stock when option prices look unusually expensive, profiting if the stock stays in a range.
iron_condor.explainer: This strategy watches a small list of U.S. stocks and checks whether their option prices are unusually expensive compared with the stock's own past year of readings, a ranking above 50 out of 100. When they are, with no earnings report due within 45 days and the market fear gauge at or below 35, it sells a four-part option trade expiring in 30 to 45 days: one put (which gains in value when the price falls) sold below the price and one call (which gains in value when the price rises) sold above it, each with a cheaper protective option bought farther away. It collects payment upfront. It closes at half the maximum profit, if the loss reaches twice the payment collected, after 21 days, or with seven days left. It trades stock options.

leader_d.name: Daily Leaders in a Weak Market
leader_d.summary: Buys daily leadership signals only while the broad market is in a downtrend, then holds for 20 trading days.
leader_d.explainer: It watches daily prices for stocks with at least a year of trading history, looking for a leadership event: a day when a stock earns a high leadership score and passes the desk's daily strength test. It acts on those events only while the S&P 500 fund SPY is in a downtrend — weakness in the broad market is a requirement, not a warning — and SPY itself is never bought by this strategy. Each event can trigger only one purchase, and it holds at most ten positions at a time. It sells each holding after 20 trading days, and a safety stop sells any holding that falls 25% below its purchase price. It trades US stocks.

leader_sc.name: Small-Cap Leaders on Weak Days
leader_sc.summary: Buys small, lightly traded stocks flagged as leaders while the broad market is falling, then holds them for about a month.
leader_sc.explainer: This strategy watches the smallest, least heavily traded tenth of stocks, measured by their average weekly trading value over the past year, and it also watches whether the broad market is in a falling period. It buys when a stock in that small-company group is newly flagged by the desk's daily leader screen during that weak market period, and only if the stock has at least a year of trading history. It holds up to ten stocks at once. It sells each stock after about 20 trading days, roughly one month, and it also places a safety exit 25% below the purchase price in case the stock falls sharply.

leaps_momentum.name: Long-Term Momentum Options
leaps_momentum.summary: Copies the desk's momentum stock picks using long-dated call options instead of shares.
leaps_momentum.explainer: This strategy watches the desk's separate momentum stock list, which holds the stocks currently favoured for their rising trends. It buys when a stock is on that list, choosing a call option, which gains in value when the price rises, with an expiry — the date the option runs out — at least a year away, priced deep below the stock's current price, and costing no more than 5% of the account for that stock. It holds up to eight stocks this way, and it may also sell short-term call options above them for extra income. It sells when a stock leaves the momentum list, when the option falls 30% from what was paid, or when under 60 days remain before that expiry date.

legends_ema.name: QQQ Trend-Day Move
legends_ema.summary: Trades only QQQ, and only after a strong trend day when its price never touched its 20-period average line.
legends_ema.explainer: This strategy watches only QQQ, a fund that tracks 100 large US technology-heavy companies, using its 15-minute price bars during regular market hours. It looks for a strong trend day: a day when the price moved mostly in one direction, covering at least about 77% of the day's full high-to-low range, and when the price never once touched its 20-period average line during that day. When both happen, it trades at the next morning's open, in the same direction as that trend day. It aims to exit at that average line, protects the trade with a stop based on half of QQQ's average daily range over the past 14 days, and closes everything by 3:59 pm Eastern.

momentum.name: Six-Month Momentum Leaders
momentum.summary: Ranks stocks by their past six months of gains and buys the strongest tenth, avoiding stressed or eventful market days.
momentum.explainer: This strategy watches a broad list of US stocks and ranks them by how much each one gained over the past 126 trading days, about six months. It buys the strongest tenth, up to ten stocks, but only from stocks priced at $5 or more that trade at least $1 million a day on average. It pauses new buys when market fear is high or jumping, around major central bank meetings, late on Fridays, and near year-end. It sells a stock if it falls 40% from its purchase price, and the list is reviewed about every 63 trading days, roughly every three months.

momentum_rotation.name: Weekly Momentum Rotation
momentum_rotation.summary: Every week, it holds the five stocks with the strongest gains over the past 60 days, in equal amounts.
momentum_rotation.explainer: This strategy watches a broad list of US stocks and ranks them by their total gain over the past 60 trading days. Once a week it buys the top five ranked stocks it does not already own, putting about 20% of the money set aside for this strategy into each one, so the five are held in roughly equal amounts. At that same weekly check, it sells any holding that has slipped below 10th place in the ranking, or that can no longer be ranked. Each purchase also carries a safety exit 25% below its purchase price in case the stock falls sharply.

morning_dip.name: Morning Dip in QQQ
morning_dip.summary: On calm, orderly mornings, it places a buy order for QQQ about one typical dip below the current price.
morning_dip.explainer: This strategy watches only QQQ, a fund that tracks 100 large US technology-heavy companies, using three-minute price bars between 10:00 am and noon Eastern. It measures how orderly the morning move has been over the last 16 bars, and it only acts when that movement is clean and directional rather than choppy. It then places a buy order one average price swing, measured over 14 bars, below the latest price. The target is the middle of the bar that triggered the setup, and a stop sits below the buy price. Unfilled orders are cancelled after nine minutes, filled trades are closed within 15 minutes, and everything is flat by noon.

phase_daily.name: Quiet Range Breakout
phase_daily.summary: Waits while a stock trades in an unusually quiet, narrow range, then buys if it breaks above that range.
phase_daily.explainer: This strategy watches stocks for quiet periods, when the daily price range squeezes unusually narrow compared with the stock's normal movement. It marks the highest and lowest prices of the first five quiet days as a box. It buys if, within the next 20 trading days, the price rises above the top of that box while the stock was already closing above its 21-day average price, and only if the price has not first fallen to the bottom of the box. It holds up to ten stocks. It sells when the price falls below a rising safety line based on the 50-day average price.

phoenix.name: Phoenix Breakout
phoenix.summary: Buys breakouts to new 20-day highs in a flat-to-weak market, waiting for the first red day to enter.
phoenix.explainer: It watches daily prices for a fixed list of 19 well-known stocks and index funds, and it also tracks the S&P 500 fund SPY as its market gauge. A buy signal forms when a stock closes above its highest close of the previous 20 days while SPY is flat or down over the trailing 60 days. It does not buy immediately: it waits for the first red day — a close below that day's open — within the next five sessions, and it stays away around company earnings reports. It sells at the close of the 20th trading day after entry, with a safety stop that sells if the price ever falls 25% below the purchase price. It trades US stocks and index funds.

qqq_put_ladder.name: QQQ Weekly Put Ladder
qqq_put_ladder.summary: Sells three cash-backed QQQ put options about once a week, far below the current price, and manages each layer as expiry — the date the option runs out — nears.
qqq_put_ladder.explainer: This strategy watches QQQ, a fund of 100 Nasdaq companies, and its put prices. The puts sit at different prices and dates, like rungs of a ladder. Once a week, if QQQ is not down over five trading days, it sells three puts expiring in 45 days, struck far below the price, so they gain value only if QQQ falls a long way (sensitivity 0.05–0.08 of 1 — near 0, it barely gains unless QQQ falls hard). Each sale is cash-backed; it holds at most 12 contracts (one contract is an option covering 100 shares). Near 21 days left, it moves a winning layer to a higher strike if QQQ rose and the put halved in value, and moves or closes a pressured layer. It buys back any put at five days left. It trades stock options.

qullamaggie.name: Leader Breakout
qullamaggie.summary: Buys the market's strongest stocks after a big run and a tight pause, when they break out in the first minutes of the day.
qullamaggie.explainer: This strategy watches stocks that rank in the top 2% for gains over the past month, three months, or six months, and that trade at least $5 million a day on average. It looks for a stock that has already risen at least 30% over about three months, then paused for 10 days in a narrow range no wider than 28%, with the range getting tighter and prices holding near their 10-day and 20-day averages. It buys when the price breaks above that pause in the first five minutes of trading. It sells a third after three or more profitable days, and sells the rest if the price falls below its stop or below its 10-day or 20-day average.

qullamaggie_paper.name: Leader Breakout — Paper Test Copy
qullamaggie_paper.summary: A paper test copy of the Leader Breakout approach that carries accepted breakout buys onto the paper account inside its own fixed budget.
qullamaggie_paper.explainer: This strategy watches the same kind of stocks as the desk's Leader Breakout strategy: strong, heavily traded US stocks breaking out of a tight pause after a big run. A separate scan prepares the possible buys and checks each one first. This test copy buys only long positions it has accepted, skips short bets, and never trades the three funds QQQ, TQQQ or GLD, which belong to another part of the desk, and never buys the same stock twice in one session. All of its buys together must fit inside a fixed $100,000 test budget. Positions it opens are then managed under the same breakout rules, including the stop price recorded with each buy. It trades US stocks.

red_day_reversal.name: Red-Day Reversal
red_day_reversal.summary: Buys strong stocks that have just had a sharp one-day drop, looking for a quick bounce within three days.
red_day_reversal.explainer: This strategy watches stocks that are still trading above their average price of the past 200 days, which keeps it focused on stocks in longer-term uptrends. It buys when a stock falls 3% or more in a single day and a short-term strength gauge called RSI, measured over two days, drops to 10 or below, a sign the selling may be overdone. It holds no more than eight stocks at once and avoids buying just before a company reports earnings. It sells when the stock rises 4% from the purchase price, falls 2% below it, or after three trading days, whichever comes first.

rsi_meanrev.name: Oversold Bounce
rsi_meanrev.summary: Buys stocks whose short-term strength gauge has fallen to an extreme low, looking for a bounce back up.
rsi_meanrev.explainer: This strategy watches US stocks for signs that recent selling has gone too far, too fast. It uses a short-term strength gauge called RSI, measured over two days, which scores a stock from 0 to 100 based on its recent gains and losses. It buys when that score falls to 10 or below. It holds no more than eight stocks at once, and each position is kept small. It sells when the stock rises 5% from the purchase price, falls 8% below it, or after five trading days have passed, whichever happens first. If none of those happen sooner, the time limit ends the trade.

rsi_meanrev_options.name: Oversold Snapback Call Spreads
rsi_meanrev_options.summary: Buys a two-part call spread when a stock in a long-term uptrend becomes extremely oversold over two days.
rsi_meanrev_options.explainer: This strategy watches U.S. stocks that are still in a long-term uptrend, with price above their 200-day average, for a sudden short-term washout. It buys a call spread, a paired option trade with limited cost and limited profit, when a very fast two-day momentum reading drops below 10, an extremely oversold level. The spread uses options expiring in 14 to 30 days, bought at or just below the current price and sold at a strike about 8% higher (the strike is the agreed price at which the option lets you buy or sell). It sells when the spread reaches half its maximum profit, when that momentum reading climbs above 70, showing the snapback has run its course, or with seven days left before expiry. It trades stock options.

rule_1d_cyan_smallcap.name: Small-Cap Pattern Signal, $5 to $10
rule_1d_cyan_smallcap.summary: Buys small companies priced between $5 and $10 when a daily pattern model flags them, then holds for about a month.
rule_1d_cyan_smallcap.explainer: This strategy watches small US companies whose shares trade between $5 and $10, that trade at least $1 million a day on average over the past 20 days, and whose total company value is below roughly $2.4 billion. A computer model scores each stock's daily price pattern, and the strategy buys only when that model raises its specific one-day flag and two of its pattern readings fall inside set ranges. If the company's value is unknown, it does not buy. It holds up to ten stocks at once and sells each one after 21 trading days, about one month, regardless of whether it has risen or fallen in the meantime.

rule_1d_green_tom.name: Turn-of-Month Momentum
rule_1d_green_tom.summary: Buys strong stocks showing a fresh daily buy signal right around the turn of the month, then holds for about three months.
rule_1d_green_tom.explainer: This strategy watches liquid U.S. stocks priced at $5 or more, with at least $1 million in average daily dollar trading over 20 days, for a strong daily buy signal. It buys at the next session's close only when three extra checks pass: the date is the last trading day of the month or one of the first three trading days of the next month, the stock's return over roughly six months is at least 65%, and a short-term price-dispersion score — how widely recent prices are spread out — sits in a narrow band between about 2.1% and 2.9%. It sells after 63 trading days, roughly three months. It trades U.S. stocks.

rule_1h_cyan_raw.name: Hourly Breakout Burst
rule_1h_cyan_raw.summary: Buys a stock for a few hours after an unusually powerful one-hour buy signal while chip stocks are trending up.
rule_1h_cyan_raw.explainer: This strategy watches a fixed basket of liquid U.S. stocks priced at $5 or more, with at least $1 million in average daily dollar trading, on one-hour charts. It buys on the next hourly bar when a strong hourly buy signal fires and that hour was exceptionally forceful: the hour's price range is at least 2.05 times the stock's typical 14-hour range, a momentum oscillator's two lines are separated by at least 6.88 points, and a major semiconductor fund is in a weekly uptrend. It sells after seven hourly bars. It holds at most ten positions at once and trades U.S. stocks.

rule_1w_cyan_mom_adx.name: Weekly Momentum Trend
rule_1w_cyan_mom_adx.summary: Buys strongly rising stocks after a weekly buy signal confirms a powerful, well-established uptrend, then holds for about six months.
rule_1w_cyan_mom_adx.explainer: This strategy watches liquid U.S. stocks priced at $5 or more, with at least $1 million in average daily dollar trading over 20 days, for a strong weekly buy signal. It buys at the next session's close only when the trend behind the signal is powerful and proven: the stock has gained at least about 44% over the past 126 trading days, a trend-strength reading is at least 25.8, which marks a firmly established trend, and the stock's trading-volume measure stays below a set ceiling. It sells after 126 trading days, roughly six months. It holds at most ten positions and trades U.S. stocks.

rule_1w_swing_beta_wt.name: Weekly High-Beta Swing
rule_1w_swing_beta_wt.summary: Buys fast-moving, market-sensitive stocks after a weekly swing signal, then holds for about six months.
rule_1w_swing_beta_wt.explainer: This strategy watches liquid U.S. stocks priced at $5 or more, with at least $1 million in average daily dollar trading over 20 days, for a weekly swing buy signal. It buys at the next session's close only when the stock tends to move much more than the broad market, moving at least 1.35 times as much as the S&P 500 fund (that market-sensitivity measure is called beta — high-beta stocks move more than the market), a momentum oscillator reading is at least 25.9, and a set of trend averages is rising with a slope of at least about 0.95%. It sells after 126 trading days, roughly six months. It holds at most ten positions and trades U.S. stocks.

snapback.name: Beaten-Down Small-Cap Snapback
snapback.summary: Buys small, beaten-down stocks that have fallen at least 20% in 13 weeks and still trade in wide daily swings.
snapback.explainer: This strategy watches the smallest, least heavily traded tenth of stocks, measured by their average weekly trading value over the past year. It looks for stocks that have fallen 20% or more over the past 13 weeks, that are not sitting right at their lowest price of the past year, and whose daily price swings over the past 20 days are among the widest in that small-company group. It buys the stocks that match all of those conditions, ranked by how wide their daily swings are. It then holds each stock for 91 days, about three months, before selling, and it waits before buying the same stock again.

spx_premium.name: Weekly Index Premium
spx_premium.summary: Sells a weekly put spread — a spread pairs a bought option with a sold one, so the most that can be made or lost is capped; premium is the payment collected for selling — on XSP, a mini S&P 500 index, priced one week of typical movement below the market.
spx_premium.explainer: This strategy watches the S&P 500 through its smaller traded version, using the prior week's closing price and its average weekly movement over 14 weeks. It sells on the first trading day of the week, at about 10 a.m. Eastern, but only if the account is worth at least $37,000 and the sale brings in a positive credit. It sells a put option (a put gains in value when the price falls) about one average weekly move below the prior close, and buys a second put 5 points lower for protection, both expiring that week. It holds the pair until the end of the week's last trading day, when both are closed for settlement. If a week's trade loses at least 90% of the 5-point width, the strategy then sits out for four weeks before selling again.

tensor_red_dip.name: Tensor Red-Day Dips
tensor_red_dip.summary: Buys strong swing signals from Tensor, the desk's pattern-scoring engine, only on fear days, when the market is down sharply and the stock itself is red too.
tensor_red_dip.explainer: It watches two things at once: how far the Nasdaq-100 fund QQQ has fallen during the day, and the fresh swing signals coming from the desk's pattern-scoring engine. It buys only on a fear day — QQQ down at least 1.5% on the day — and only when the stock itself is also down that day and its signal carries a confidence score of at least 7. It holds at most five positions at a time. It sells as soon as any one of three things happens: the stock rises 3% from the purchase price, falls 8% from it, or the third trading day after purchase arrives. It trades US stocks.

tensor_swing.name: Tensor Swing
tensor_swing.summary: Buys high-confidence swing setups, graded by Tensor, the desk's pattern-scoring engine, on fearful red days — dips in rising stocks and reversals after deep falls.
tensor_swing.explainer: It watches hourly price charts across its stock universe, using a pattern-scoring engine that grades each stock for swing setups such as pullbacks and reversals. It puts a stock forward as a buy only when the engine's confidence score reaches at least 7, the stock is not held, and it has not run too far and turned euphoric. Before any buy goes through, the wider desk applies its own checks: the day must be broadly red and fearful, the setup must fit a dip in a rising stock or a reversal after a deep fall, and a person reviews the chart. This strategy has no sell rule of its own: it only puts forward buys, and holdings are closed by the desk's separate position checks. It trades US stocks.

ts_momentum_decile.name: One-Year Momentum Top Tenth
ts_momentum_decile.summary: Once a month, it buys the tenth of stocks with the best one-year gains, spread evenly and with no single industry taking over.
ts_momentum_decile.explainer: This strategy watches a broad list of US stocks and ranks them by their gain over the past 252 trading days, about one year. Once a month it buys the top tenth of that ranking, but only from stocks with at least a year of history that trade at least $1 million a day, and it leaves out stocks with a suspicious pattern of long flat periods followed by an extreme jump. The money is spread evenly across the chosen stocks, and no single known industry group is allowed to make up more than a quarter of the holdings. It has no price-based stop; instead, it sells any stock that drops out of the top tenth at the next monthly check.

vix_hedge.name: Market Crash Insurance
vix_hedge.summary: Buys long-dated call options on a volatility fund when markets are calm, as insurance against a sudden crash.
vix_hedge.explainer: This strategy watches the market's fear gauge, which tracks expected stock-market swings. When markets are complacent, with the gauge below 16 or sitting in its lowest quarter of the past 30 days, it buys call options (a call gains in value when the price rises) on a volatility fund that tends to jump when fear spikes. The options expire in 60 to 110 days, aimed near 90, with a strike price — the agreed price at which the option lets you buy or sell — about 20% above the fund's current price, and the position is kept small at about 1% of the account. It sells if the options double in value, if the fear gauge spikes above 30, or when 21 days remain before expiry. It trades stock options.
